<reason>CON built a cleaner, more damaging line of attack that PRO never fully neutralized: the "who checks the checker" dilemma (agencies writing their own discrepancy memos under criteria they authored) and the timing/manipulation point introduced in Rebuttal 2 (a trader can profit politically by moving the price during the live decision window regardless of eventual settlement outcome). PRO's answers—position limits, disclosure, "preannounced quality criteria," and the tu quoque that expert panels face the same theater objection—were competent but left the core asymmetry (open, cross-examinable expert deliberation vs. after-the-fact defensive memos about an unaccountable price) largely intact. PRO's closing conceded manufactured doubt as merely "a cost of scrutiny" rather than defeating it, effectively conceding CON's sharpest live point. CON's opening being clipped is a real execution cost, but the substantive framing had already landed before the cut, and CON's subsequent rounds (Pressure Questions and Rebuttal 2 especially) sharpened rather than repeated the case, giving it the clearer path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A1 in Rebuttal 2 ([A4.1]-[A4.2]), arguing that manipulation only needs to move the price during the live decision window—not win at settlement—to force officials to spend political capital rebutting manufactured doubt, was the most decisive exchange; PRO's response (subsidy/position-limit design fixes) addressed settlement-profit incentives but never squarely answered the interim-window damage claim.</best_rebuttal>
